chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from some of our companions, from Ubayd ibn Zurara who said: Hamza ibn Humran narrated to me, saying:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about capability (al-istita'a), but he did not answer me. So I went to him another time and said: 'May God keep you well! Something from it has settled in my heart that nothing will remove except something I hear from you.' He said: 'Whatever was in your heart will not harm you.'

I said: 'May God keep you well! I say: God, Blessed and Exalted, does not burden His servants with what they are not capable of, and does not burden them except with what they can endure, and they do not do anything from that except by God's intention, His desire, His decree, and His pre-determination.' Then he said: 'This is the religion of God which I and my forefathers follow.'

key_terms.إرادة: God's intention or will — the immediate divine will that encompasses each action
key_terms.الاستطاعة: Capability, ability, or power to perform an action — the central theological concept of this hadith, debated by all Islamic schools
key_terms.قدر: God's pre-determination — divine foreordainment or measure of all things
key_terms.قضاء: God's decree — the determined ordinance or judgment of God
key_terms.مشيئة: God's desire — broadly synonymous with will, sometimes distinguished as the broader dispositional will

ai.seo_question: What is the Shia theological position on free will and divine decree (al-istita'a)?
ai.summary: This hadith presents a creedal dialogue between Hamza ibn Humran and Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) on the fundamental theological question of al-istita'a (capability or free will). Hamza initially received no answer, reflecting the Imam's caution in addressing a highly contested topic in early Islamic theology — a debate between the Mu'tazilites (who emphasized human free will) and the Jabrites (who denied it altogether). The Imam ultimately affirms the 'middle path': God does not burden people beyond their capacity (refuting determinism that denies moral responsibility), yet all human actions occur within the framework of God's will, intention, decree, and pre-determination (refuting pure free-will that denies divine sovereignty). This doctrine — sometimes called 'amr bayna amrayn' (a matter between two extremes) — is the distinctive Shia theological position.
